No one expected writer-director George Lucas's film to be a hit. The studio bosses were so convinced that the film, "a science fiction Western" whose main cast was unknown (Harrison Ford, Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher), would flop that they graciously handed Lucas, free of charge, the merchandising rights to any product related to Star Wars. Obviously, they did not expect it to generate 5 sequels, three "prequel" chapters, a spin-off based on the Ewoks, cartoons, computer games, toys, soundtracks, books, huge video and DVD sales, candy, clothing, bedding and even food (and countless parodies, notably three specific Star Wars episodes of the cartoon Family Guy). The film cost $11 million and grossed more than $460 million, but it did not seem to have the potential to become a huge hit.

But Lucas had big dreams. Two decades before computer imagery was used to create fantastic worlds, the visionary director, using ultra-detailed models, clever tricks and well-chosen locations, told the story of another universe. The evil Empire, dominated by Darth Vader (David Prowse, with the voice of James Earl Jones), is in control; the rebel forces are gathering to try to overthrow the tyrants.

Lucas created a mythology that was enthusiastically embraced by people of all ages. Besides giving rise to various creatures from a galaxy far, far away, his good-versus-evil storyline introduced us to people, phrases and concepts that have since become part of the collective consciousness: the Millennium Falcon (Han Solo's spaceship, which Lucas originally imagined looking like a flying hamburger), lightsabers (the sword-like weapon with its distinctive sound), the Imperial stormtroopers ("May the Force be with you") and, of course, the Jedi knights (today such an integral part of our collective unconscious that an internet campaign urging people to answer "Jedi" to a question about religion on a United Kingdom census form was hugely successful).

By bringing Star Wars to life, Lucas managed to create much more than just a film. He created a world, a new style of filmmaking and an unforgettable space opera that has never been surpassed.

block_special.description:
No director since Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980) has captured the delicious voyeurism of horror as well as John Carpenter does in Halloween, a film so full of our most primal anxieties that it still defines the genre 20 years later. Indeed, the comparison between Hitchcock and Carpenter is no exaggeration: Halloween is full of Carpenter's tributes to Hitchcock, from the characters' names - Sam Loomis and Tom Doyle, from Psycho (1960) and Rear Window (1954), respectively - to the casting of Jamie Lee Curtis (b. 1958), daughter of Janet Leigh (1927-2004), the unfortunate shower victim of Psycho.

Halloween's plot is quite simple: a masked psychopath, Michael Myers, stabs and strangles his way through a group of teenage friends as they drink beer and chase after sex, until he finally comes up against the film's great pure force, the virginal babysitter Laurie Strode (Curtis). Despite its minimalism, the evident social anxieties of good versus evil in Halloween's plot are left unresolved at the end, a strategy repeated consistently in other slashers ranging from Friday the 13th (1980) to Scream (1996). The intensity of Carpenter and of Debra Hill's (1950–2005) screenplay lies in placing horror in the placid setting of suburban American life, where young people are presumed (or at least were once presumed) to be safe.

Deconstructing the notion of the home as a protected place, Halloween's camerawork invades the fictional town of Haddonfield with a roaming point-of-view shot. The film opens with a brilliant shot showing everything through the eyes of the killer, then six years old. Carpenter builds a purely aesthetic fear, setting Halloween apart from its own tiresomely expository offspring. Throughout the film, someone is always watching, whether predator or prey. As the film unfolds, we find ourselves lurking around corners, behind shoulders, through windows and through cracks in closet doors, waiting for what we believe to be certain death.

The brilliant pacing and excruciatingly long takes keep the adrenaline high as Michael slinks through the shadows, cheating death several times to stalk the smart Laurie. When the film ends, we are left anxiously wondering what separates fact from fiction.

block_special.description:
"In space no one can hear you scream." The tagline on the Alien poster was an obvious come-on, but there was plenty of screaming in theaters. Defying the popularity of Star Wars (1977), Ridley Scott (b. 1937) resurrected the cheap genre of scary monsters from outer space, paired it with a meticulous, big-budget look and created a paralyzing science fiction horror film capable of leaving nerves completely frayed.

Dan O'Bannon's sophisticated screenplay owes a great deal to the ingenious 1950s B movie Giant from the Unknown (1958) and follows the "haunted house" formula of The Cat and the Canary (1939) or Ten Little Indians (1965), but set aboard a spaceship and with a much greater gross-out factor.

The Nostromo is a gigantic cargo ship operating in deep space, with a minimal (and far from conventional) crew led by Captain Dallas (Tom Skerritt) that includes the smart Lieutenant Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) and Jones the cat. Responding to a distress call, they discover an abandoned alien ship and strange eggs. As they examine the eggs, a parasite leaps out of one and latches onto Kane's (John Hurt) helmet, infecting him and, a few days later, wreaking terrifying havoc when a baby alien bursts out of his chest during breakfast. The other actors supposedly didn't know what was going to happen, which made their shock and revulsion genuine.

Scott creates a frisson and uses the dark corridors dramatically as the dwindling crew - who apparently never watched a horror film as teenagers - walks straight into the monster's pair of extendable jaws. What raised the anguish to an art form, through Oscar-winning visual effects, was the unparalleled art direction and design, blending organic and metallic patterns, as well as the (only glimpsed) alien designed by the artist H. R. Giger, whose terrible beauty was given an eerie grace by the statuesque Maasai dancer Bolaji Badejo.

Weaver became a star and an icon overnight as the brave survivor Ripley, facing her final battle in nothing but a T-shirt and underwear. She was supposed to end the film naked, to emphasize human fragility in the face of the perfect killing machine, but 20th Century Fox, eager to avoid an "R" rating (restricted for those under 17) in the United States, vetoed the idea. Unusually for a horror franchise, the sequels were handed to directors famous for their distinctive visual styles - James Cameron, David Fincher and Jean-Pierre Jeunet.

block_special.description:
This potential contender for a Golden Turkey Award in the "kitsch" category ended up becoming one of the big hits of 1984, and its enduring popularity has enshrined it as a classic of the genre. The Terminator is a triumph of style over plot, of cleverness over intelligence, and a combination of elements that adds up to more than the sum of its parts. Its circular narrative about the future's attempt to control the past in order to take control of itself, thereby changing the premises of its own state, is familiar to every fan of postwar science fiction literature (Harlan Ellison, Philip K. Dick, and others) and of postwar television series (such as The Outer Limits and Star Trek).

Shortly after completing low-budget special effects for Roger Corman (b. 1926) and John Carpenter (b. 1948), writer-director James Cameron (b. 1954) adopted his mentors' disarming humor to shield himself from objections about the many plot holes. The vision of a bleak, dark, apocalyptic future was fashionable at the time, as attested by Escape from New York (1981), by John Carpenter, Mad Max (1979), by George Miller (b. 1945), Le dernier combat (The Last Battle, 1983), by Luc Besson (b. 1959), and Forbrydelsens Element (The Element of Crime, 1984), by Lars von Trier (b. 1956).

Cameron's assured style (tech noir, as it was called after a nightclub in the film) and his kinetic energy combined with narrative economy keep the viewer distracted from the absurdity of the whole thing. Even Arnold Schwarzenegger, the epitome of bad acting with his cold facial expression, heavy Austrian accent, and body language learned at the same school as Frankenstein's monster, becomes a major triumph for the film. The casting, Cameron admitted to Wired magazine, "shouldn't have worked. The guy is supposed to be an infiltrator, and it's impossible not to spot him immediately in a crowd, unless everyone looked like Arnold". Nevertheless, everyone who has seen this unlikely phenomenon knows most of the film's lines by heart, including Schwarzenegger's peculiar pronunciation. "I'll be back" is probably the most quoted line of all, often used as a catchphrase on radio and television shows.

If The Terminator's ability to engage its audience recalls the fan cult of The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), its insistent irony points ahead to the jokes of the Scream series (1999-2011), built on generic clichés. The same can be said of the sadistic violence and the heroine's turnaround at the end. Beneath the surface of this cut-and-paste of science fiction elements lies an even less original slasher movie, featuring a (literally) mechanical killer and a tough heroine (Linda Hamilton) who discovers her capacity to fight back and combat evil. The film's appeal, as with all great films, does not come from its supposed originality. It is the way Cameron brings together familiar elements and breathes new life into them that results in such a memorable experience, one that ultimately changed science fiction films in theaters forever.

block_special.description:
In the 1960s, teen movies had Frankie Avalon (b. 1940), Annette Funicello (b. 1942), lots of sand (and no sex) and upbeat music, while in the 1970s being a teenager essentially meant getting slaughtered in your bed in a string of horror films. But in 1984, writer-director John Hughes revolutionized the genre with Sixteen Candles, which he followed the next year with The Breakfast Club, a film whose great achievement was finally showing teenagers as they really talk and think.

No other film summed up the period better, or became more of a cult favorite among teenagers, than The Breakfast Club. It made Hughes a name to watch closely - he went on to make the excellent Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986) and the hugely successful Home Alone (1990) - and it brought together a talented group of young actors (just as Francis Ford Coppola's The Outsiders had done two years earlier) whom the media dubbed the "Brat Pack".

Five very different teenagers are suspended and must serve Saturday detention for various reasons. Despite their differences when the day begins, they end up bonding with one another. We have the school jock (Emilio Estevez), the weirdo with too much eyeliner (Ally Sheedy), the stuck-up princess (Molly Ringwald, teen idol and Hughes's muse ever since she starred in Sixteen Candles), the nerd (Anthony Michael Hall) and the rebel (Judd Nelson), all trying to keep themselves entertained under the watchful eye of the complex teacher Mr. Vernon (Paul Gleason).

This film, which relies on a screenplay of witty one-liners rather than on action, works largely thanks to the cast's characterizations as truths are revealed, resentments are voiced and each of them gets a turn to shine. Although copied in films and TV series, it may well be the definitive teen movie, whether for its perfect timing, its sharp performances, its quotable lines or its time-capsule-worthy 1980s soundtrack, which includes the classic "Don't You Forget About Me" by Simple Minds, written for the film.

block_special.description:
Writer-director Oliver Stone (b. 1946) was the first Vietnam veteran to get Hollywood backing to make an autobiographical film about the conflict. The Deer Hunter (1978) and Apocalypse Now (1979) had turned the war into subject matter for movies, but it was Platoon that showed the reality of Vietnam to generations who only came of age after the conflict was over.

Chris Taylor (Charlie Sheen), who stands in for Stone, is an idealistic young man who volunteered to serve with the infantry in Vietnam. He feels torn between two "fathers": the gentle, sensitive super-soldier Sergeant Elias (Willem Dafoe), who smokes pot and listens to soul with the Black soldiers, and the sadistic, scar-faced Sergeant Barnes (Tom Berenger), who drinks and listens to country and western with the rednecks. Chris follows the path of other screen soldiers, "becoming a man", but whereas the recruits whipped into shape by John Wayne always ended up saluting the flag, Chris ends up losing faith in his country amid the blood and confusion.

Although it is overly schematic in pitting the two sergeants against each other and contrasting their philosophies, Platoon is a powerful film. Terrifying as he is, Barnes teaches Chris how to survive rather than become a martyr - the climax, unthinkable in earlier films, has Chris shooting one of his own superiors rather than facing the enemy. Harrowing and suspenseful as it is, the film is not devoid of nostalgia - the soundtrack is made up of big 1960s hits and, in one scene, the soldiers sing "The Tracks of My Tears" by Smokey Robinson & The Miracles.

block_special.description:
In one of the first scenes of the 1988 film Who Framed Roger Rabbit, the human protagonist, detective Eddie Valiant, played by Bob Hoskins (b. 1942), is drinking at a bar when he is approached by a local jerk. The guy starts needling Valiant about his choice of clients, asking who he was working for that week: "Goofy? Or Screwy Squirrel?". Valiant kicks his tormentor's stool out from under him. Gripping the man's head in his hands and shaking with rage, he growls: "Get this, meatball: I - don't - work - for - toons!".

But, as you probably know, not only does Valiant work for toons, but the success of Who Framed Roger Rabbit soon made the rest of Hollywood want to work for them too. When that film cast human actors alongside a bunch of rubbery, spring-loaded, violent cartoon characters, it was taking a huge risk: the film went about $28 million over budget, attempting technical feats of animation that had never been done before to make the cartoons and humans look as if they were really shooting and grabbing each other. But it paid off, grossing $156 million and winning three Oscars.

Roger Rabbit was far from the first film to feature cartoons and humans crossing the, well, color line. Cab Calloway (1907-1994) made appearances in Betty Boop cartoons such as Minnie the Moocher (1932), some of which opened with live-action footage of the Cotton Club bandleader dancing before revealing a version of him rotoscoped into an animated ghost. By the 1940s, animation technology was good enough for humans to share the screen with cartoons, so Gene Kelly could tap-dance with Jerry the mouse in Anchors Aweigh (1945). But Roger Rabbit broke new ground, even beyond Jessica Rabbit's curves: it proved to film studios not only that audiences loved human-cartoon mash-ups, but that cartoons in general could make a lot of money.

Imitators followed, and joint cartoon-human productions became a fruitful genre between the late 1980s and the mid-1990s. Like Roger Rabbit, these subsequent productions were tinged with racial messages, the tension (sexual or otherwise) between flesh and blood / pen and ink flickering with the danger and thrill of miscegenation. Toontown is a depraved but lovable ghetto in danger of being razed; in the 1989 music video for Paula Abdul's "Opposites Attract", she sings a duet with a cartoon feline character called MC Skat Kat. "It's no fiction / just a natural fact", they whisper. "We come together / because opposites attract".
block_special.credits: Summary based on the article "When Hollywood Went to Toontown", by Madeline Leung Coleman on topic.com.

reviews.review_description: E Christopher Nolan fez mais uma vez, entregou uma obra-prima que como muitas outras obras, divide opiniões.

A Origem (Inception, 2010) não é nenhuma esfinge. Na verdade, a sua estrutura, emprestada dos filmes-de-assalto, é bem trivial. Acompanhamos o planejamento de um golpe enquanto se aprende o essencial de cada personagem. Na hora de pôr o golpe em prática, termina o ensaio, começam os imprevistos.

Em 2000, Christopher Nolan surpreendeu o mundo ao lançar Amnésia. Seu grande atrativo era a engenhosidade de roteiro e edição, que permitia que a trama fosse contada, literalmente, de trás para frente. Era um exercício de talento de um diretor ainda iniciante e, ao mesmo tempo, um desafio aos espectadores. Uma década depois, Nolan repete a proeza com A Origem. Só que em níveis bem mais ousados.
Nolan is exploring dreams and the possibilities are endless, which is why it’s a little disappointing that so much of the film feels like a…

I even think its dexterous complexity is at least partially downwind of some cultural Stockholm syndrome re: complexity as legitimacy in the tradition of things…

reviews.review_description: Lembro-me claramente a primeira, e até recentemente única vez que assisti A Rede Social. À época, não usava a ferramenta e mesmo hoje tenho minhas reservas pessoais. De toda forma, tenho a vívida memória de ter saído do cinema totalmente de queixo caído. Essa impressão perdurou ao longo dos anos e, agora, quando finalmente revi o oitavo filme de Fincher para elaborar a presente crítica, ela foi reconfirmada em sua integralidade, talvez até ampliada.

Sabe aqueles filmes que começam mal pacas? Acredite. A Rede Social começa de forma impecavelmente chata, talvez, para mostrar o quão controversa é a figura de Mark Zuckerberg, criador do Facebook, um fenômeno da internet. Será?

Leave it to David Fincher and Aaron Sorkin to make the development of Facebook and the terrible minds behind it so riveting.
Una perfecta metáfora de la conversión de un mundo agotado en una globalización internauta donde triunfan nuevos procesos de socialización.

Suspense espacial de Alfonso Cuarón encanta-se com a fragilidade e a tenacidade humanas

O universo é hostil. Sem oxigênio, sem som, no vácuo, ele não oferece a menor condição de sobrevivência à vida humana caso esteja fora deste planeta azul chamado Terra. As breves visitas do homem neste ambiente inóspito são sempre repletas de aparatos desenvolvidos para garantir sua existência, por mais que eles em muitos casos estejam longe do confortável. Foi exatamente com este cenário em mente, de desconforto e do risco constante, que o diretor Alfonso Cuarón conceituou Gravidade. Um filme que impressiona pela ousadia, tanto de narrativa quanto estética, sem jamais deixar de lado o clima de tensão.
This is virtuoso film-making on every level.
With its themes of spirituality, religion, birth, rebirth and hope, Gravity is a film that will move audiences in different ways.

reviews.review_description: Mesmo com uma filmografia tão curta (apenas 3 filmes), Steve McQueen há muito tempo já mostrou a que veio. Tanto em Fome quanto em Shame, filmes de temáticas tão distintas entre si, o diretor traz em seu estilo seco, cru e realista uma forma de ressaltar as nuances de suas obras, experiências desconfortáveis e difíceis, porém sempre sinceras naquilo que querem retratar. Com 12 Anos de Escravidão não é diferente, com McQueen atingindo seu ponto máximo enquanto realizador.

A saída da sessão para a imprensa e indústria de 12 Anos de Escravidão (12 Years a Slave) no Festival de Toronto era como uma procissão de lamentos. Poucas pessoas conversavam e a maioria enxugava as lágrimas. Algumas seguiam chorando minutos após o fim do filme.

12 Anos de Escravidão chega aos cinemas aproximadamente 126 após a abolição da escravatura no Brasil, que ocorreu com a Lei Áurea de 1888. Os Estados Unidos acabaram com a escravidão algumas décadas antes, em 1863, mas em um processo bem mais conflituoso, que gerou uma guerra que dividiu o país.
Ambitious, honest and horrifying all at once, 12 Years a Slave may not be the easiest film to watch more than once, but it will…

did_you_know_list.title: Three days of shooting
did_you_know_list.description: The first known adaptation of Mary Shelley's novel, the film was shot in just three days in January 1910 at Edison's studios in the Bronx, New York.

did_you_know_list.title: A monster in reverse
did_you_know_list.description: To create the monster, the crew burned a dummy while moving its arms and head, then ran the footage backwards so the creature seemed to rise from the ashes.

did_you_know_list.title: Toned-down horror
did_you_know_list.description: Edison announced that the film deliberately avoided the novel's repulsive situations in order to focus on the story's mystic and psychological aspects.

did_you_know_list.title: A pioneering blockbuster
did_you_know_list.description: With 5,000 extras, lavish sets and a running time of about two hours, the Italian film was one of the first blockbusters in history and set the standard for epics for decades.

did_you_know_list.title: Crowds in the audience
did_you_know_list.description: At its Berlin premiere in March 1913, the crowd scenes were reinforced by costumed actors performing live inside the auditorium.

did_you_know_list.title: Inspired by Alice Guy
did_you_know_list.description: Phalke decided to make films in 1911 after watching Alice Guy's The Life of Christ (1906) in Bombay: seeing Jesus on screen, he pictured the Hindu gods Rama and Krishna instead.

did_you_know_list.title: A pea plant as a test
did_you_know_list.description: Lacking investors, Phalke filmed a pea plant in a pot, one frame a day for over a month, and showed the result to persuade backers.

did_you_know_list.title: A landmark of Indian cinema
did_you_know_list.description: It is considered the first Indian feature film. Being silent, it had intertitles in English, Marathi and Hindi.

did_you_know_list.title: Two Pompeiis in one year
did_you_know_list.description: In 1913 Italy released two different adaptations of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's novel: this one, by Ambrosio, and another produced by Pasquali.

did_you_know_list.title: Disputed direction
did_you_know_list.description: The film was directed by Eleuterio Rodolfi. Mario Caserini is sometimes co-credited, but on uncertain grounds: the Italian magazine Bianco e Nero mentions only Rodolfi.

reviews.review_description: The series start shows Fantomas in disguise and Juve's obsession with capturing him.
For something that's now 97 years old, it's a terrific, hugely entertaining film.

did_you_know_list.title: An instant hit
did_you_know_list.description: The five-episode serial was hugely popular in France and made René Navarre, who played Fantômas, an overnight celebrity.

did_you_know_list.title: Suspense without surprise
did_you_know_list.description: Audiences already knew the plot from the serialized novels, so the interest lay in how the story would unfold rather than in what would happen next.

did_you_know_list.title: Restored in 2006
did_you_know_list.description: The five episodes, released in 1913 and 1914, were restored under the direction of Jacques Champreaux and re-released in 2006.

quote.quote: There is nothing in this involved, compact, and concentrated film but explosive genius.
quote.author: Maurice Raynal, critic (Chronique cinématographique, 1914)

reviews.review_description: Essa liberdade de movimento transforma a narrativa numa experiência de fluidez refinada, onde cada transição revela algo impressionante.
Fire effects, a volcanic eruption, battles, thrilling adventures on land and water, crowds of actors make a kaleidoscope of action that lasts for more than…
Cabiria is a great conception, and it has been wonderfully realised.
Cabiria is in every sense of the word a genuine masterpiece, and undoubtedly the very last word in dramatic photo visualization.

did_you_know_list.title: The Cabiria shot
did_you_know_list.description: The film popularized the tracking shot with the camera on a dolly, moving towards and away from the scene. For years, cameramen called this movement the "Cabiria shot".

did_you_know_list.title: Words by D'Annunzio
did_you_know_list.description: Writer Gabriele D'Annunzio wrote all the intertitles, named the characters and gave the film its title.

did_you_know_list.title: Maciste is born
did_you_know_list.description: Cabiria marks the debut of Maciste, the muscular slave who became the hero of dozens of Italian films in the following decades.

reviews.review_description: Miss Bara as the vampire scores easily.
The "Vampire" has been given an inimitable interpretation by Theda Bara...
The old fashioned drama is creaky and if judged just in modern terms, it doesn't pass the giggle test.

did_you_know_list.title: The birth of the vamp
did_you_know_list.description: The film popularized the word vamp (short for vampire) for a femme fatale who seduces and ruins her victims. Theda Bara is credited simply as "The Vampire".

did_you_know_list.title: An invented biography
did_you_know_list.description: At a 1915 press conference, the studio presented Theda Bara as an exotic Arabian actress and then deliberately leaked that it was all a hoax: one of Hollywood's first publicity stunts.

did_you_know_list.title: Banned in Britain
did_you_know_list.description: Although part of the story is set in England, the film was rejected by the British censors, who banned illicit sexual relationships on screen.

did_you_know_list.title: Distorting mirrors
did_you_know_list.description: To show the scientist's hallucinations, Abel Gance used distorting mirrors and ordinary lenses, since distorting lenses did not yet exist.

did_you_know_list.title: "He's crazy"
did_you_know_list.description: Gance recalled that, after seeing the film, the producers decided he was crazy and should not be trusted with another penny.

reviews.review_description: To describe in detail the marvelous workings as depicted by the Messrs.
The filming of Jules Verne's immortal story has been capitally and, from a photographic viewpoint, at times, wonderfully done.
The struggles of the men against the undertow and the force of the water proved interesting, while the battle between the unarmed pearl diver and…

did_you_know_list.title: The first underwater feature
did_you_know_list.description: It was the first feature film shot underwater. The scenes were made in the Bahamas with a system of watertight tubes and mirrors that reflected the images to the camera.

did_you_know_list.title: The photosphere
did_you_know_list.description: For the octopus fight, John Ernest Williamson devised the "photosphere", a steel globe holding the cameraman, connected to a boat by a submarine tube.

did_you_know_list.title: Too expensive
did_you_know_list.description: The film took two years to make and cost $500,000, so much that, according to Hal Erickson, it put a stop to new Verne adaptations for 12 years.

did_you_know_list.title: Almost entirely lost
did_you_know_list.description: Only about one minute of the film is known to survive today. The rest is lost.

did_you_know_list.title: Egypt in California
did_you_know_list.description: Replicas of the Great Pyramid and the Sphinx were built in Ventura County, California. The production had 15,000 extras and more than 2,000 horses.

did_you_know_list.title: Censors' scissors
did_you_know_list.description: Theda Bara's daring costumes led censorship boards, such as Chicago's, to demand cuts in several of the queen's scenes.

did_you_know_list.title: An answer to Griffith
did_you_know_list.description: The film was conceived as a response to The Birth of a Nation (1915), to counter the racist stereotypes of Griffith's film.

did_you_know_list.title: A project transformed
did_you_know_list.description: It was meant to be a short to accompany Griffith's film, but lack of money delayed it for more than two years, and much footage about Black achievements was cut.

did_you_know_list.title: Bad timing
did_you_know_list.description: Released in December 1918, weeks after the end of World War I, it failed at the box office: audiences no longer wanted to see war films.

did_you_know_list.title: A landmark of Black cinema
did_you_know_list.description: It is believed to be the first feature made with a Black cast and crew for a Black audience, the first of the so-called race movies, and Oscar Micheaux's directing debut.

did_you_know_list.title: Funded by farmers
did_you_know_list.description: To fund the film, based on his own novel, Micheaux sold stock in his company to white farmers around Sioux City for $75 to $100 a share.

did_you_know_list.title: A Selznick star
did_you_know_list.description: It was the first film Olive Thomas, a former Ziegfeld Follies star, made for the newly formed Selznick Pictures, which reportedly paid her $2,500 a week.

did_you_know_list.title: A lavish launch
did_you_know_list.description: To promote the film, the Selznicks put up two electric signs in Times Square and released a song of the same title, with the actress's photo on the sheet music.

did_you_know_list.title: A lost film
did_you_know_list.description: The film is now presumed lost.

movies.original_title: The Symbol of the Unconquered: A Story of the Ku Klux Klan

did_you_know_list.title: Against the Ku Klux Klan
did_you_know_list.description: Released only a few years after The Birth of a Nation, the film was advertised precisely for its negative depiction of the Ku Klux Klan.

did_you_know_list.title: A rare survivor
did_you_know_list.description: It is Oscar Micheaux's fourth feature and, together with Within Our Gates, one of the few films from the director's early period that survive.

reviews.review_description: A Carlitos, é atribuído o valor da mudança catalizada pela presença do garoto.
Formerly it was the custom to say that Mr. Chaplin played down to the level of his audiences.
The Kid is less uproarious than later Chaplin efforts, serving more as a testing ground as it offers a charming yet tough-minded tale.
Those constant contenders who maintain that Charlie Chaplin is the master mummer of the movies and the world's greatest actor, either in the silent or…

did_you_know_list.title: A smuggled negative
did_you_know_list.description: During his divorce from Mildred Harris, who was trying to seize his assets, Chaplin smuggled the negative to Salt Lake City and edited the film in a hotel room.

did_you_know_list.title: The first child star
did_you_know_list.description: The film turned Jackie Coogan, then a vaudeville performer, into the movies' first major child star.

did_you_know_list.title: A personal film
did_you_know_list.description: It was Chaplin's first feature as director. Shooting began ten days after the death of his infant first son, which may explain the tenderness between the Tramp and the boy.

reviews.review_description: O ato final impressiona pelas belíssimas imagens suspensas, evidenciando a altura de onde Lloyd está pendurado.
Lloyd is generally considered the most prosaic of the era’s comedic “big three,” lacking Chaplin’s poetry and Keaton’s deadpan genius.
There are some brilliant slapstick sequences and there’s also great character work which emphasizes that, for truly skilled actors, spoken dialogue is far from a…

did_you_know_list.title: An illusion of height
did_you_know_list.description: The climb was filmed on the roofs of several buildings of different heights in downtown Los Angeles, with sets matching the facade of the main building.

did_you_know_list.title: Inspired by a steeplejack
did_you_know_list.description: The sequence was inspired by Bill Strother, a steeplejack Lloyd saw climbing a building, who plays "Limpy" Bill in the film.

did_you_know_list.title: A secret stuntman
did_you_know_list.description: Lloyd did most of his own stunts, but stuntman Harvey Parry also took part in the climax, a secret he revealed only after the actor's death.

reviews.review_description: Os Dez Mandamentos ( título que DeMille refilmaria, em 1956 ) é uma produção ambiciosa que marcou época e influenciou gerações de cineastas.
Whether to witness a piece of Old Hollywood history that’s quite literally still being rediscovered or because the film speaks to your faith, there’s a…
This is light years better than the Heston version.
DeMille's trademark sensibility aside, the two sections illustrate what the director gave up in his transformation into epic moviemaker.

did_you_know_list.title: The audience's idea
did_you_know_list.description: DeMille ran a contest with the Los Angeles Times to choose the film's subject. Eight entrants suggested the Ten Commandments, and each received $1,000.

did_you_know_list.title: Two stories
did_you_know_list.description: The film has a biblical prologue about the Exodus, with Technicolor scenes, and a modern story about two brothers with opposing views of the commandments.

did_you_know_list.title: Remade by DeMille himself
did_you_know_list.description: In 1956, DeMille remade the film with sound, this time focusing solely on the story of Moses.

quote.quote: You cannot break the Ten Commandments—they will break you.
quote.author: F. C. Nelson, winner of DeMille's story contest

reviews.review_description: Lang's direction is consistent, and achieves plasticity, dignity, and very nearly power.
This silent classic is a technical wonder for the day.
The producers seem to have been mistaken in going in for straight drama rather than for romance and magic.

did_you_know_list.title: A mechanical dragon
did_you_know_list.description: The dragon Siegfried fights was a huge mechanical puppet operated by technicians hidden inside it, one of the most ambitious effects of German cinema at the time.

did_you_know_list.title: A two-part epic
did_you_know_list.description: Written by Thea von Harbou from the medieval poem the Nibelungenlied, Lang's epic was released in two parts in 1924: Siegfried and Kriemhild's Revenge.

reviews.review_description: With its overabundance of slow motion and overly written subtitles, it would be a better picture if cut to 15 or 20 minutes.
Margarethe Schön persuasively passed from being lovesick to hate-fuelled in a display of duality than anticipated Maria and the Robot's in Metropolis.
Thankfully the spectacular ending – all done with life size sets, which left Lang and his team no option but to pull it off in…

did_you_know_list.title: The second half
did_you_know_list.description: Kriemhild's Revenge premiered two months after Siegfried, in 1924, and follows the hero's widow seeking vengeance at the court of Attila, king of the Huns.

did_you_know_list.title: A familiar face
did_you_know_list.description: Attila is played by Rudolf Klein-Rogge, who was also Dr. Mabuse and the inventor Rotwang in Metropolis, both by Fritz Lang.

did_you_know_list.title: A ballet intermission
did_you_know_list.description: The Dada short was made to be shown during the intermission of Francis Picabia's ballet Relâche, with music by Erik Satie, which premiered in Paris in December 1924.

did_you_know_list.title: An avant-garde cast
did_you_know_list.description: Francis Picabia, Erik Satie, Marcel Duchamp, Man Ray and René Clair himself all appear in the film.

reviews.review_description: No cinema, o uso de suas ideias gerou um curta-metragem de grande carga poética, porém curiosa, a começar pelo título, Balé Mecânico (1924).

did_you_know_list.title: A painter directs
did_you_know_list.description: The film was conceived by Cubist painter Fernand Léger and co-directed by filmmaker Dudley Murphy, with cinematographic input from Man Ray.

did_you_know_list.title: A separate score
did_you_know_list.description: George Antheil's score was written for the film, but its premiere, in Vienna in September 1924, was a silent version.

did_you_know_list.title: Paul Robeson's debut
did_you_know_list.description: It was Paul Robeson's film debut, at 27, in a dual role. He was paid $100 a week plus three percent of the gross after the first $40,000.

did_you_know_list.title: Censored
did_you_know_list.description: New York's censors found the film immoral and sacrilegious. Micheaux had to re-edit it twice, cutting it from nine to five reels; the original version is lost.

reviews.review_description: With Flesh and the Devil benefiting from an easy meshing of its cast’s palpable subjective feelings with its own form, the film’s depiction of its…
Miss Garbo is hereafter a star to be reckoned with, so perfectly does she create a character for the heroine, lovely, pitiful, thrilling Felicitas, who…
Greta Garbo is at her best.

did_you_know_list.title: Garbo didn't want it
did_you_know_list.description: Greta Garbo refused to make the film: she was exhausted and grieving her sister's death. She agreed only after a stern letter from MGM threatening dire consequences.

did_you_know_list.title: A real romance
did_you_know_list.description: The chemistry between Garbo and John Gilbert was not faked: the two began an affair during filming and moved in together before production ended.

did_you_know_list.title: Found in a storehouse
did_you_know_list.description: Considered lost for 45 years, the film was rediscovered by its director, Teinosuke Kinugasa, in his storehouse in 1971.

did_you_know_list.title: Actors did everything
did_you_know_list.description: Kinugasa nearly went bankrupt making it: the actors slept on the set, painted scenery, made props and pushed the camera dolly.

did_you_know_list.title: Famous names
did_you_know_list.description: Future Nobel laureate Yasunari Kawabata is credited with the original story. Eiji Tsuburaya, later the effects creator of Godzilla, also worked on the film.

did_you_know_list.title: A director replaced
did_you_know_list.description: Mauritz Stiller, Greta Garbo's mentor, started directing the film but struggled with the Hollywood studio system and was replaced by Fred Niblo.

did_you_know_list.title: Two endings
did_you_know_list.description: Louis B. Mayer found the ending so depressing that he ordered a happier alternate one. Theatres could choose which ending to show.

did_you_know_list.title: Invented history
did_you_know_list.description: The comedy mixes fictional incidents with real historical figures such as Abraham Lincoln, Brigham Young and Sitting Bull.

did_you_know_list.title: A forgotten comedian
did_you_know_list.description: Its star, Raymond Griffith, was one of the great silent comedians. In 2005 the film was added to the US Library of Congress's National Film Registry.

reviews.review_description: As a work of art it is a complete failure, because it is anaemic and because it shows us a Christ who, though obviously a…
In a genre that deserves the best artists can offer but is plagued by mediocrity, DeMille's flawed but powerful film remains one of Hollywood's most…
This King of Kings is beautiful. I am astonished at the acumen of the producer, of the director.

did_you_know_list.title: Instead of Noah
did_you_know_list.description: DeMille planned an epic about the Flood but gave up on learning that Warner Bros. was preparing Noah's Ark. A writer then suggested the story of Jesus.

did_you_know_list.title: Colors and tints
did_you_know_list.description: The opening and resurrection were shot in two-color Technicolor; other scenes were tinted, and the torches in Jesus' arrest were hand-colored.

reviews.review_description: Unfortunately, the salesgirl who is supposed to have "it" must strike educated beholders as a rather vapid hoyden.
It is smart, funny and real. It makes a full-size star of Clara Bow and it hits William Austin out of the minor class into…

did_you_know_list.title: The it girl is born
did_you_know_list.description: The film made Clara Bow a star and popularized the term "it girl": "it" being the magnetic quality that draws all others.

did_you_know_list.title: $50,000 for an idea
did_you_know_list.description: Paramount paid writer Elinor Glyn $50,000 for the concept. She appears in the film as herself, explaining what "it" is.

did_you_know_list.title: A Gary Cooper cameo
did_you_know_list.description: A young Gary Cooper appears briefly as a reporter, shortly before becoming a star.

reviews.review_description: As usual in Hugo, love is measured in sacrifice, yielding a sincere and extravagant sense of romance.
I have never seen a better representation of the spirit of a novel in that the picture not only interprets the lusty romantic feeling of…
Conrad Veidt does a wonderful piece of acting.

did_you_know_list.title: Meant for Lon Chaney
did_you_know_list.description: Universal offered the role to Lon Chaney but failed to secure the book rights in time. Released from it, Chaney chose to make The Phantom of the Opera (1925) instead.

did_you_know_list.title: The grin behind the Joker
did_you_know_list.description: Gwynplaine's disfigured grin, played by Conrad Veidt, is cited as a visual inspiration for Batman's villain the Joker.

quote.quote: The Man Who Laughs is a melodrama, at times even a swashbuckler, but so steeped in expressionist gloom that it plays like a horror film.
quote.author: Roger Ebert, critic

reviews.review_description: For some time past I have been nourishing the secret hope that the jazz-mad, gin-soaked younger generation had vanished from the screen.

did_you_know_list.title: A star is born
did_you_know_list.description: The film launched the career of Joan Crawford, as a Jazz Age flapper.

did_you_know_list.title: Sound without dialogue
did_you_know_list.description: There is no audible dialogue: the film was released with a synchronized score and sound effects, on disc and on film.

did_you_know_list.title: A censor's cut
did_you_know_list.description: The Kansas censor board ordered the cut of the intertitle "Before I met you, Norman—before I knew anything about love—things happened."

did_you_know_list.title: A farewell poem
did_you_know_list.description: Robert Desnos read the poem that inspired the film at a farewell dinner before leaving for Cuba. Man Ray promised to finish the film before his friend returned.

did_you_know_list.title: Images through glass
did_you_know_list.description: Man Ray used a gelatin plate process to give the images a textured-glass look, which also helped get the nude scenes past the censors.

did_you_know_list.title: Before Buñuel
did_you_know_list.description: Released in 1928, a year before Un Chien Andalou, Germaine Dulac's film from Antonin Artaud's script anticipated techniques later associated with surrealist cinema.

did_you_know_list.title: Baffled censors
did_you_know_list.description: The British Board of Film Censors reported the film was "so cryptic as to be almost meaningless. If there is a meaning, it is doubtless objectionable".

did_you_know_list.title: The first all-talkie
did_you_know_list.description: It is the first all-talking feature film. It cost $23,000 and grossed over $1 million.

did_you_know_list.title: It grew in secret
did_you_know_list.description: It was meant to be a two-reel short, but with the Warner brothers away in Europe the crew kept expanding the plot and shot four more reels than agreed.

reviews.review_description: A figura rude do pai está muito bem representada por David Torrence, que consegue ser insensível e bruto na medida certa.
Murnau's sense of evocative image and editorial rhythm greatly elevates it.
It has one of those stories that are aimed at the sentimentality in a person but never quite reach their mark.
Its first part is a beautiful, powerful story of the love of a city waitress and a son of the wheatlands...
Nadie puede dudar que F. W. Murnau fue uno de los grandes maestros del cine.

did_you_know_list.title: Our daily bread
did_you_know_list.description: The working title was Our Daily Bread, the name the film kept in Brazil. It was shot on location in Oregon in 1928.

did_you_know_list.title: A silent made to talk
did_you_know_list.description: Shot as a silent, it was refitted with some dialogue and released in 1930 as a part-talkie because audiences had lost interest in silent films. That sound version is lost.

did_you_know_list.title: Director in hospital
did_you_know_list.description: While scouting locations in August 1928, Murnau had appendicitis and underwent emergency surgery in Pendleton.

reviews.review_description: Despite its flaws, the film remains a fascinating souvenir of a vanished avant-garde.
A surrealist burst of artistic angst...

did_you_know_list.title: The Orphic Trilogy
did_you_know_list.description: It is the first part of Jean Cocteau's Orphic Trilogy, which continues with Orpheus (1950) and ends with Testament of Orpheus (1960).

did_you_know_list.title: Lee Miller's only role
did_you_know_list.description: Photographer Lee Miller made her only film appearance here. The film was financed by patron Charles de Noailles.

did_you_know_list.title: Church cinema
did_you_know_list.description: Written and directed by Spencer Williams, the religious film was made on a tiny budget with amateur actors for the Black community's circuit of theatres and churches.

did_you_know_list.title: Preserved
did_you_know_list.description: In 1991 it became the first race film selected for the US Library of Congress's National Film Registry.

did_you_know_list.title: The first Technicolor film
did_you_know_list.description: It was the first film made in Technicolor and the first feature-length color film produced in the United States, using a two-color, red and green process.

did_you_know_list.title: A special projector
did_you_know_list.description: Showing it required a special projector with two lenses and two filters. Because the images were hard to align, it was the only film made with that first system.

did_you_know_list.title: Lost in a fire
did_you_know_list.description: The only known print was destroyed in a fire in 1961. Only very short fragments survive.

reviews.review_description: Fairbanks is in reliably athletic, charismatic form as the sole survivor of a ruthless pirate attack who manages to infiltrate the marauders’ own criminal ranks…
The beautiful colors of this picture and the minute attention to detail make them seem like animated "Old Masters" in parade.
The Black Pirate is wholly -- to steal a phrase from Juno and the Paycock -- a darling film.

did_you_know_list.title: Restrained colors
did_you_know_list.description: Douglas Fairbanks feared color would distract and tire audiences, so he avoided Technicolor's saturated tones and used a restricted palette for the all-color film.

did_you_know_list.title: Pirates demand color
did_you_know_list.description: Since 1922 Fairbanks had said it would be impossible to film a pirate story satisfactorily in black and white, because pirates "suggest colour to the imagination".

reviews.review_description: Sternberg's richly ornamental compositions-which are dense with shadows and objects that separate viewers from the action-suggest a willful distance from his characters.
Josef von Sternberg's Underworld is a fascinating early cornerstone of both the director's worldview and the gangster genre.
Few filmmakers in the history of cinema have invoked the inherent eroticism of the image like Sternberg...

did_you_know_list.title: An Oscar for the story
did_you_know_list.description: Based on a story by former Chicago crime reporter Ben Hecht, the film won him the Academy Award for Best Original Story at the first Oscar ceremony.

did_you_know_list.title: A comeback
did_you_know_list.description: After setbacks at MGM and with Chaplin, Sternberg accepted work as an assistant director at Paramount. His work stood out and the studio gave him Underworld, which made his name.

did_you_know_list.title: A seed of noir
did_you_know_list.description: It is considered one of the first gangster films and a forerunner of film noir.

reviews.review_description: Walt Disney e Ub Iwerks criaram o impossível e, no meio do caminho de suas carreiras, conseguiram, genialmente, alcançar o sucesso.
Steamboat Willie... introduces a new cartoon character, henceforth to be known as "Micky Mouse." It is an ingenious piece of work with a good deal…
It's a peach of a synchronization job all the way, bright, snappy and fitting the situation perfectly.
Charming and beautifully made, these early animated films provide a window into the past.

did_you_know_list.title: Mickey's official debut
did_you_know_list.description: It is considered the official debut of Mickey and Minnie, although both had already appeared in Plane Crazy and The Gallopin' Gaucho, which had not found a distributor.

did_you_know_list.title: The Jazz Singer effect
did_you_know_list.description: Disney decided to make a fully synchronized sound cartoon after seeing The Jazz Singer (1927). To do so, he used a click track to keep the timing.

did_you_know_list.title: Not the first
did_you_know_list.description: Contrary to popular belief, it was not the first sound cartoon: the Fleischer brothers made 19 sound cartoons between 1924 and 1926, though without full synchronization.

reviews.review_description: Vencedor do Oscar de Melhor Filme em 1930, Melodia da Broadway é possivelmente a pior produção a levar o prêmio para casa.
Although the audible devices worked exceedingly well in most instances, it is questionable whether it would not have been wiser to leave some of the…
If all the songs and ballets were taken out of The Broadway Melody it would still remain an absorbing spoken drama.
Though derided by some as a hopelessly outdated relic, the first musical Oscar winner for Best Picture remains a surprisingly gritty and daring romantic triangle…

did_you_know_list.title: The first talking Best Picture
did_you_know_list.description: It was the first sound film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture and one of the first musicals with a Technicolor sequence, sparking a trend for color in the musicals of 1929–1930.

did_you_know_list.title: Learning to record
did_you_know_list.description: The crew learned to record sound by trial and error: sets were modified and scenes reshot. Bessie Love's brief ukulele scene took more than three hours to film.

did_you_know_list.title: A silent version

did_you_know_list.title: Third Cinema
did_you_know_list.description: Its directors, Fernando Solanas and Octavio Getino, published the manifesto "Towards a Third Cinema", which influenced Latin American political filmmaking.

reviews.review_description: Conta com inesquecíveis imagens ao som da cultura brasileira que, como um quebra cabeça, monta este epílogo da história de Antônio das Mortes.

did_you_know_list.title: Cannes prize
did_you_know_list.description: Glauber Rocha won the Best Director award at the 1969 Cannes Film Festival.

did_you_know_list.title: Antônio das Mortes returns
did_you_know_list.description: The cangaceiro killer Antônio das Mortes, played by Maurício do Valle, had already appeared in Black God, White Devil (1964).

did_you_know_list.title: A first color film
did_you_know_list.description: It was Glauber Rocha's first color film.

reviews.review_description: Ultimately [Sergio] Leone’s epic of the Mexican revolution is a portrait in disillusion grounded in ambiguity and contradictions and the most eccentric and touching friendships…
As with most Leone works, A Fistful of Dynamite (which also made the rounds under the monikers Duck, You Sucker and Once Upon a Time…
The film is overlooked, missing big name stars, and released with numerous different titles since its premiere, but it's still a memorable entry in Leone's…

did_you_know_list.title: A reluctant Leone
did_you_know_list.description: Sergio Leone intended only to produce the film, but ended up directing after other directors fell through.

did_you_know_list.title: The Mexican Revolution
did_you_know_list.description: Leone's last western as director, the film is set during the Mexican Revolution, with Rod Steiger and James Coburn.

reviews.review_description: The Green Berets simply will not do as a film about the war in Vietnam.
Simplicities of the right, simplicities of the left, but this one is beyond the possible. It is vile and insane.
The film’s serious moments are tough to bear, but its sense of humor is worse.

did_you_know_list.title: In favor of the war
did_you_know_list.description: John Wayne directed and starred in the film to defend the Vietnam War, at a time when American public opinion was turning against it.

did_you_know_list.title: The sun in the wrong place
did_you_know_list.description: At the end, the sun sets over the sea to the east of Vietnam, a geographical error often pointed out by critics.

did_you_know_list.title: A real case
did_you_know_list.description: Nagisa Oshima based the film on a real case of a family that used their son to fake traffic accidents and extort drivers.

did_you_know_list.title: Across Japan
did_you_know_list.description: The family travels Japan from north to south running the scam, giving the film a road-movie feel.

reviews.review_description: Claire's Knee is a movie for people who still read good novels, care about good films, and think occasionally.
A more perfect inauguration and encapsulation of warm weather...
Love, sex, fetishism, and objectification all receive verbal workouts in this witty and wise enterprise.

did_you_know_list.title: A moral tale
did_you_know_list.description: It is the fifth of Éric Rohmer's "Six Moral Tales", a series of films about temptation and fidelity.

did_you_know_list.title: Lake Annecy
did_you_know_list.description: The film was shot on the shores of Lake Annecy, in the French Alps, with cinematography by Néstor Almendros.

reviews.review_description: On some dumb fundamental level, Airport kept me interested for a couple of hours. I can't quite remember why.
Hayes provides wonderful comic relief as Ada Quonsett (that name!).
Before there was Airplane! there was Airport, a surprisingly engaging disaster drama that ignited a trend.

did_you_know_list.title: Father of disaster movies
did_you_know_list.description: The film's success kicked off the 1970s wave of disaster movies and spawned three sequels.

did_you_know_list.title: An Oscar for Helen Hayes
did_you_know_list.description: Helen Hayes won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress as an elderly stowaway.

did_you_know_list.title: From swords to fists
did_you_know_list.description: Jimmy Wang Yu wrote, directed and starred in the film, one of the first to swap swords for bare-handed combat, paving the way for the kung fu boom.

did_you_know_list.title: Shaw Brothers
did_you_know_list.description: The film was produced by Hong Kong's Shaw Brothers studio.

reviews.review_description: Visconti's mastery of visual style almost succeeds in creating the very ideas and feelings that his heavy-handed narrative entirely misses.
Visconti takes the veneer and calls it furniture. With infinite tedium, he pores over every facet of Tadzio's Botticelli visage.
“Death in Venice” is a film about humanity’s slow transcendence into nothingness and everything.

did_you_know_list.title: Mahler instead of a writer
did_you_know_list.description: Visconti turned the writer of Thomas Mann's novella into a composer modeled on Gustav Mahler, whose music dominates the soundtrack.

did_you_know_list.title: Cannes prize
did_you_know_list.description: The film received the 25th Anniversary Prize at the 1971 Cannes Film Festival.

reviews.review_description: For that 80% of the film which constitutes the story, the structure and dialog create a mood of nervous terror which the other 20% nearly…
Eastwood displays a vigorous talent for sequences of violence and tension.
While it’s hardly (Eastwood's) best directed film, you get good tastes of the filmmaker he would become all throughout “Misty”.

did_you_know_list.title: Eastwood's debut
did_you_know_list.description: It was the first film directed by Clint Eastwood, shot in Carmel, California, where he lived.

did_you_know_list.title: A Don Siegel cameo
did_you_know_list.description: Director Don Siegel, Eastwood's mentor, makes a small appearance as a bartender.

reviews.review_description: Scripter Frank Pierson with director Sidney Lumet has injected broadly comic aspects and the laughs work without reducing suspense.
Carries the unfortunate burden of echoing other, better films.
Unfortunately, failed comedy and vigorous suspense are handcuffed together for the entire trip.

did_you_know_list.title: Surveillance everywhere
did_you_know_list.description: Sidney Lumet's film shows a heist planned while the gang is recorded by various surveillance agencies, a theme that anticipated Watergate.

did_you_know_list.title: Christopher Walken's debut
did_you_know_list.description: The film marks one of Christopher Walken's first screen appearances.

reviews.review_description: That Mon Oncle Antoine is such a fine film only underlines the tragedy of the director's later life...

did_you_know_list.title: Canada's best
did_you_know_list.description: In several critics' polls, it has been voted the greatest Canadian film of all time.

did_you_know_list.title: The director in the cast

did_you_know_list.title: The Australian New Wave

did_you_know_list.title: A Williamson play

reviews.review_description: The picture would be more fun if we cared about who got killed and who survived.
What the glittering, star-driving survivalism of Poseidon Adventure actually presents is a nightmarishly schematic fantasia of guiltless discomfort.
Neither as exciting nor as unintentionally funny as one would like it to be.

did_you_know_list.title: An upside-down ship

did_you_know_list.title: Beresford's debut
did_you_know_list.description: It was Bruce Beresford's first feature and a big hit of the new Australian cinema.

reviews.review_description: Images is not remotely an example of hack work -- it's an example of a conceptual failure.
Images is a masterpiece of mental and sexual disquietude.
Committed contributions from York (acting), Zsigmond (photography), Williams (score), and Yamash'ta (sound design) amount to little more than a jangling jumble of hyperbolic head games.

reviews.review_description: The placement of an old-fashioned Dracula in a modern black neighborhood is a great idea, but amateurish production leaves Marshall stranded in the film.

did_you_know_list.title: An African prince

did_you_know_list.title: Blaxploitation horror

did_you_know_list.title: Crime in Quebec

did_you_know_list.title: Roger Moore's debut

reviews.review_description: This pompously prophetic thing of a film hasn’t a brain in its beanbag.
Soylent Green is Edward G. Robinson's movie. As a man who remembers the wonders of civilization before it died, he is witty, cultivated and endlessly…
Its greatest attribute is not that it accurately anticipated many things about humanity's future.

did_you_know_list.title: The future is 2022

The music quickly becomes monotonous, and the operatic dialogue is silly right from the start.
The music had imprinted itself on me in ways that proved inescapable.

did_you_know_list.title: Shot in Israel

did_you_know_list.title: Diola resistance

did_you_know_list.title: All in an inn

did_you_know_list.title: Sammo Hung's choreography
did_you_know_list.description: The fights were choreographed by Sammo Hung, who would become one of the great names of Hong Kong action cinema.

reviews.review_description: Hondo's passionate, wide-ranging voice-over commentary, addressing the hero in the second person, blends confession and observation, aspiration and despair, societal and personal conflicts.
A combination of pure documentary and improvisation, the film lacks a conventional plot but offers instead many gripping scenes.
Nearly every piece of the film truly feels inspired and where sure there is the occasional scene that feels a bit too on the nose…

did_you_know_list.title: Golden Leopard
did_you_know_list.description: The first feature by Mauritanian director Med Hondo, about an African immigrant in Paris, shared the Golden Leopard at the 1970 Locarno Festival.

did_you_know_list.description: Hondo shot the film over several years, on weekends and with little money, while working as an actor and dubbing artist.

reviews.review_description: With this film, Wenders crystallized his style of existential sentimentality.
A breakthrough for Wenders, codifying the dreamy, sentimental existentialism that became his signature.
"Something changes you when you drive around America," Vogler explains to his boss. Wenders transposes this aching, nameless restlessness to West Germany.

did_you_know_list.title: The road trilogy
did_you_know_list.description: It is the first film of Wim Wenders's "road trilogy", followed by Wrong Move (1975) and Kings of the Road (1976).

did_you_know_list.title: Polaroids
did_you_know_list.description: The protagonist, a journalist, photographs everything with a Polaroid, trying to capture what he sees during his trip across the United States.

reviews.review_description: O Enigma de Kaspar Hauser é excelente em todos os aspectos e a história é intrigante por completo.
Kaspar Hauser is one of the most fascinating of films. At his best, Herzog is like no other film-maker I know.
In Herzog's dedication to film art he denies us the simple pleasures of story involvement, of suspense, of interest in the people on the screen…
Thematically similar to the Herzog classics Fitzcarraldo, Aguirre, the Wrath of God, and Grizzly Man, it is yet another portrait of a seemingly demented hero…

did_you_know_list.title: A real case
did_you_know_list.description: The film tells the true story of Kaspar Hauser, a young man who appeared in Nuremberg in 1828 after spending his life locked in a cellar.

did_you_know_list.title: Bruno S.
did_you_know_list.description: The lead, Bruno S., was a street performer who had spent much of his life in institutions. Herzog discovered him in a documentary.

reviews.review_description: Ao longo dos 98 minutos, Noite do Terror é se apresenta como um bom filme do subgênero slasher .
Fascinating as opposed to wholly enjoyable, Bob Clark's Canadian sorority house slasher is largely gore-free, but bolsters the anaemia with a genuinely disturbing tone that…
Made in 1974, this effective Canadian stalk'n'slash movie mixes dark humour with sinister tension.

did_you_know_list.title: A slasher forerunner
did_you_know_list.description: The Canadian film is considered one of the forerunners of the slasher genre and anticipated devices used in Halloween (1978).

did_you_know_list.title: From the same director
did_you_know_list.description: Director Bob Clark would later make the Christmas comedy A Christmas Story (1983).

reviews.review_description: The point of this sort of movie seems to be to arouse outrage without offending anyone.
“The Parallax View” is a gripping thriller that will keep viewers on the edge of their seats, eagerly anticipating each new twist and turn in…
Fifty years after its release, The Parallax View holds up as a political thriller depicting the 1970s paranoia.

did_you_know_list.title: The paranoia trilogy
did_you_know_list.description: It is the second film of Alan J. Pakula's "paranoia trilogy", between Klute (1971) and All the President's Men (1976).

did_you_know_list.title: Gordon Willis's cinematography
did_you_know_list.description: The cinematography is by Gordon Willis, also of The Godfather, known as the "Prince of Darkness".

reviews.review_description: A cold, heartless, and deadening picture.
The film can be confusing at times since it seems to go in too many directions but Morley's portrayal is bewitching.

did_you_know_list.title: A cop duo

did_you_know_list.title: Wrecked cars
did_you_know_list.description: The film became known for its spectacular chases, including a car flying into an apartment.

reviews.review_description: Perhaps there is something in its very crassness, horror and tastelessness that does at least jolt us towards an acknowledgment of pure evil.
The Night Porter is a doomsday vision of sex.
The positions of torturer and victim slip around and into each other, and this is presented as part of the violence itself—a violence that continues…

did_you_know_list.title: Controversy
did_you_know_list.description: Liliana Cavani's film, about the relationship between a former SS officer and a concentration camp survivor, caused huge controversy and was censored in Italy.

did_you_know_list.title: Charlotte Rampling
did_you_know_list.description: The image of Charlotte Rampling in a Nazi cap and suspenders became one of the most remembered of 1970s cinema.

reviews.review_description: Throughout, Hearts and Minds displays more than enough heart. It is mind that is missing.
A cry of despair made by a person whose viewpoint hadn't yet been soundly vindicated.
Filmmaking-wise, it should be forever celebrated for its inspired and highly influential editorial structure.

did_you_know_list.title: A controversial Oscar
did_you_know_list.description: The Vietnam War documentary won the Oscar. Accepting it, producer Bert Schneider read a telegram of greetings from Vietnamese representatives, causing controversy at the ceremony.

did_you_know_list.title: A Johnson phrase
did_you_know_list.description: The title comes from President Lyndon Johnson's line about the need to win the "hearts and minds" of the Vietnamese people.

reviews.review_description: The Cars That Ate Paris is both part of that and a carnivalesque reflection of it.
The whole thing is played too broadly, but home-improvement victims will appreciate the unending weeks it takes for a simple bathroom to be converted into…

did_you_know_list.title: Peter Weir's debut
did_you_know_list.description: It was Peter Weir's first feature; he would later direct Picnic at Hanging Rock and Witness.

did_you_know_list.title: Parallel cinema
did_you_know_list.description: The film is a landmark of Indian "parallel cinema", realist and political, far from Bollywood formulas.

did_you_know_list.title: Co-directed
did_you_know_list.description: It was co-directed by Volker Schlöndorff and Margarethe von Trotta, then married.

With impeccable detail and merciless wit, John Schlesinger’s The Day of the Locust presents 1930s Los Angeles as a nightmarish circle in Dante’s Inferno.
The most impressive aspect of Schlesinger’s film is its sense of place: the sunny, awesomely relaxed, fetid warmth captured by Conrad Hall’s sumptuous cinematography.

did_you_know_list.title: 1930s Hollywood
did_you_know_list.description: The film adapts Nathanael West's novel about Hollywood's misfits during the Great Depression.

did_you_know_list.title: Homer Simpson
did_you_know_list.description: One of the characters is called Homer Simpson, a name Matt Groening later said came from his own father rather than the book.

reviews.review_description: The film is... a very effective fable.

did_you_know_list.title: An Ira Levin novel
did_you_know_list.description: The film adapts the novel by Ira Levin, also the author of Rosemary's Baby.

did_you_know_list.title: A popular expression
did_you_know_list.description: The title gave rise to the expression "Stepford wife", used in English for a submissive wife with no will of her own.

reviews.review_description: Sholay is a grand, maximalist revel. It's the kind of movie that, while it may pass into the status of so many older movies more…
You can divide Hindi cinema into two eras, pre-and-post Sholay. It is a landmark. They don't make 'em like this anymore.
Sholay covers every base, works all the emotions, and even today, when Amitabh Bachchan and Dharmendra show up, thunderous ovations result.

did_you_know_list.title: Five years in theatres

did_you_know_list.title: A comedian producer
did_you_know_list.description: Comedian Rudy Ray Moore funded the film with money from his comedy records, basing it on the character he created on stage.
